chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umeyr, from Ammar ibn Marwan, who said:

I said to Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him), 'My father was visited by death, so he was told to bequeath. He said, 'This is my son' — meaning Umar — 'so whatever he does, it is valid.' Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) said to him, 'Your father has bequeathed and has been concise.' I said, 'He ordered such and such for you.' He said, 'It is valid.' I said, 'And he bequeathed the emancipation of a believing, knowledgeable slave-girl. When we emancipated her, it became clear to us that she was not of sound judgment (minor).' He said, 'It is valid for him. The example of that is like a man who buys a sacrificial animal on the understanding that it is fat, but finds it thin. It is valid for him.'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling if a bequeathed slave-girl is found to be a minor upon emancipation?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Al-Kafi*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) validates the father's general bequest of his son's judgment, illustrating the Shia legal principle that a testator's intent is respected even if the specific object of the bequest has a latent defect. The analogy of the sacrificial animal (*udhiyah*) being thinner than expected underscores that minor imperfections do not invalidate the fulfillment of the religious or legal obligation, provided the core requirement is met. This reflects the broader Shia jurisprudential emphasis on the validity of actions based on the presumed soundness of the testator's knowledge unless proven otherwise.
